# Code conventions — Services Team

**Use when:** you are about to write or change any application code — before the first line, not at review time.

How the code in this repository is written. `.s7/shared/engineering-rules.md` says what must be true of a delivery; this file says what must be true of the code. Every story in this pack follows it: US-002.

The repository's stack is not recorded on this pack, so take the naming style, the test command and the project layout from the files already in it rather than from any default.

## 1. Read this repository before you write in it

1. **The repository outranks this file.** Before writing a line, open the two or three files nearest the change — the neighbouring module, its tests, the layer above it — and follow what they already do: naming, file layout, how errors travel, how things are wired together, how tests are arranged. Where this repository disagrees with the guidance below, the repository wins, and the story note says which file set the precedent.
2. **Match the existing seams.** If the codebase separates its web layer from its services and its services from its data access, a new criterion enters at the same layer and calls down the same way. Do not introduce a new architectural pattern inside a story; that is an architecture decision, and it belongs to `.s7/shared/architecture.md` and a conversation, not to a diff.
3. **Reuse before you add.** Search for an existing helper, client, validator or fixture before writing another one. A near-duplicate of something already in the repository is a defect, not a shortcut.

## 2. Naming

4. Names say what a thing **is or does**, in this repository's own vocabulary and the domain's — `eligibility`, `plan sponsor`, `claim`, not `data`, `info`, `manager`, `helper`, `util`, `process`, `handle`.
5. Follow the naming style already in the files you are editing, and never mix two styles in one file. A name that needs a comment to be understood is the wrong name.
6. No abbreviations a newcomer would have to decode, no single letters outside a short loop or a lambda, and no type names smuggled into identifiers.

## 3. Size and shape

7. **A function does one thing and reads top to bottom.** If you cannot describe it in one sentence without "and", split it. If a reader has to scroll to hold it in their head, split it.
8. **Keep nesting shallow.** Return early on the failure paths and leave the main path flat and unindented, rather than wrapping the body in ever-deeper conditionals.
9. **A class or module has one reason to change.** When a story keeps adding unrelated methods to the same type, that type is now two types.
10. Keep the public surface small: expose what the criterion needs and keep everything else private to the module. A narrow surface is what makes the next story cheap.

## 4. Errors

11. **Never swallow a failure.** No empty catch, no bare `except`, no returning a default because something went wrong. Handle it, or let it travel to a caller that can.
12. Handle a failure where there is enough context to do something meaningful, and say what the code will do about it: fall back, retry once, or fail the request. The acceptance criterion decides which, and if it does not say, that is an open question to ask rather than a decision to guess.
13. **Error messages name what failed and what to do about it.** No apologies, no bare stack traces reaching an end user, and never a raw internal detail in a message the browser will show.
14. Fail loudly at the boundary and quietly in the middle: validate once on the way in, then let the inner code trust its own types.

## 5. Validation and boundaries

15. **Validate at the edge, once.** Every value crossing into the application — a form field, a request body, a query parameter, an uploaded file, a message off a queue — is checked at the point it arrives, and everything inside works on values already known to be good.
16. Never build a query, a path, a command or markup by pasting strings together with user input. Use the parameterised form the stack already provides, and never turn validation off to make a test pass.
17. A criterion about an invalid input is a criterion about a **message the user sees**, so it needs the same test and the same evidence as the happy path.

## 6. Logging

18. Log the events that would let someone reconstruct what happened: the decision taken, the boundary crossed, the failure caught. Do not log a line per statement, and do not leave debugging output behind.
19. **Log identifiers, never contents** — a claim reference, never the claim; a member id, never the member. No personal data, no credentials, no tokens, no request bodies. This is not a style rule.
20. Use the levels the repository already uses, and use the failure level only for something a person must act on. A log line that fires on every request at a level someone is paged for is a defect.

## 7. Comments and documentation

21. **Comments say why, never what.** The code already says what it does; a comment earns its place by recording the reason, the constraint or the rejected alternative that is not visible in the syntax.
22. Give a docstring or its equivalent to anything another module calls, describing the contract rather than restating the signature. Private helpers with good names need nothing.
23. **A comment that has gone stale is worse than no comment.** If a change makes one wrong, fix it in the same diff.

## 8. What never ships

24. **No dead code**: nothing unreachable, nothing commented out, no function no caller reaches, no import nothing uses. Deleting it is safe — the history has it.
25. **No speculative abstraction**: build what the criterion in hand needs and no more. An interface with one implementation, a parameter nothing varies, a hook nothing calls and a configuration switch nothing sets are all cost with no user.
26. **No unfinished markers left silently.** A `TODO` ships only when it names a follow-up recorded in the story note; anything else is either done now or is not in scope.
27. **Nothing generated by guesswork.** No invented method on a library that may not have it, no dependency added to make an example compile, no code copied from elsewhere whose behaviour you have not read. If you are unsure a call exists, check it before you write it.
28. **No secrets, ever** — connection strings, keys and tokens come from the environment, never from source, a fixture, a test or a committed configuration file.

## 9. Dependencies

29. Prefer what is already available: the language's own library, then a package the repository already depends on. A new third-party dependency is a decision the team takes, not a convenience a story adds — it needs a line in the story note saying what it does and why nothing already present would do.
30. When a new dependency is genuinely needed, it goes in the one minimal manifest hunk the git workflow allows, pinned to an exact version, in its own commit named for the story.

## 10. The code is part of the criterion

31. A criterion is met when its test passes **and** the code that makes it pass follows the rules above. The plan in the story note names the functions this criterion needs, so the diff should hold those and little else — a change nobody planned is either an omission to record or scope creep to stop.
